1.title: Designing Accessible Public Consultation Notices that Engage Communities
1.content: Consultation Notice project for Weston Consulting
1.subtitle: Weston Consulting
1.overview:
As part of Weston Consulting’s Community Consultation initiatives, this project focused on redesigning the Public Consultation Notice, a document distributed to residents within designated city areas to inform them about upcoming developments. The goal was to create a modern, approachable, and fully AODA-compliant design that communicates clearly to all residents, regardless of ability. 

By refining hierarchy, layout, and typographic structure, the new system balances accessibility with visual clarity, ensuring complex planning information feels transparent and easy to navigate. Printed on recyclable stock and mailed directly to households, the redesigned notice set a new benchmark for clarity, inclusivity, materiality, and civic communication, turning a procedural document into a meaningful tool for community engagement.
1.context:
The Public Consultation Notice redesign emerged from Weston Consulting’s broader effort to make community engagement more accessible and visually coherent. Working alongside planners and the design team, I participated in the design, accessibility research, and production of a notice system that translates technical planning information into clear, approachable communication for residents. 

The process involved developing accessible typography, colour, and layout structures fully aligned with AODA standards, ensuring the notices could be easily read by all audiences. I also created maps, icons, and visual templates to establish a consistent framework that could be adapted across multiple city projects. Each element was tested for legibility, contrast, and clarity, resulting in a scalable system that balanced civic transparency with thoughtful design.
1.problem:
Previous Public Consultation Notices were dense, text-heavy, and visually outdated. Layouts lacked structure, and accessibility standards were inconsistently applied, resulting in documents that were functional but often overlooked because of the complexity of the information. The format failed to engage residents or communicate complex planning information clearly, especially for readers with visual or cognitive impairments. 

The task was to design a fully accessible, visually clear, and modular system that met AODA and WCAG 2.1 standards while remaining practical for in-house teams to reproduce and adapt. Beyond compliance, the goal was to create a design that invited participation, strengthened public trust, and reflected Weston Consulting’s commitment to inclusive, environmentally responsible communication.
1.research:
Designing for accessibility, understanding, and trust. Through review of existing notices, accessibility documentation, and feedback from past consultations and resident surveys, we identified several recurring challenges in how information was presented to the public, from unclear hierarchies, visual clutter and inconsistent formatting to complex technical drawings and information. 

Legibility became the foundation for every design decision. Large type, generous spacing, and clear sectioning improved readability across audiences, while a set of custom icons I created helped simplify complex information. Simplified maps replaced technical diagrams to help residents locate sites easily and understand proposals at a glance. To make the notices both sustainable and practical for internal printing, I proposed using recyclable paper and embedding QR codes for extended content online. This solution reduced material waste and ensured each notice remained easy to reproduce and distribute directly from the office.
1.process: Designing accessibility as an information outlet. The process followed a research-driven structure that moved from accessibility compliance and information clarity toward sustainable production and delivery. Each phase aimed to transform the Public Consultation Notice into an approachable, trustworthy, and operationally efficient communication tool for both residents and staff.
1.solution:
The Public Consultation Notice established a new standard for civic communication, an accessible system that translates complex planning information into clear, approachable language and layout. Each element was designed with legibility and inclusivity in mind: optimized for comfortable reading, contrast ratios refined for accessibility, and structure built to guide residents naturally through key details. 

Custom icons and simplified maps improve navigation and understanding, while the integration of QR codes extends engagement beyond print, connecting residents directly to online resources and feedback portals. The use of recyclable paper and a streamlined in-office production process ensured that the notice was not only accessible but also environmentally responsible. What emerged is a framework that balances clear, sustainable, and fully AODA-compliant design. Now adopted across Weston’s community engagement materials, it reinforces trust, transparency, and accessibility in every consultation.
1.impact:
The Public Consultation Notice transformed how residents interact with municipal planning information. By combining accessibility standards, clear hierarchy, and visual clarity, the notices became not only easier to read but more engaging, evidenced by a 40% increase in interactions using QR code and portal, compared to previous static formats. Feedback from residents and municipal partners highlighted improved comprehension and confidence, reinforcing the importance of inclusive design. Beyond immediate usability, the project established a repeatable system that can scale across future community consultation initiatives. The use of recyclable materials demonstrated that accessibility and environmental responsibility can coexist, setting a new standard for sustainable municipal communications. 

Through this process, I learned how design can translate technical and regulatory requirements into meaningful experiences. Balancing AODA compliance with visual clarity, informational structure, and user-centred thinking showed me that accessibility is not a limitation, it is a creative opportunity. This project strengthened my understanding of designing for diverse audiences, building systems that endure, and connecting residents to their communities in ways that are both practical and engaging.
technologies: Design: Adobe Illustrator, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe InDesign
Accessibility & Standards: AODA, WCAG 2.1, Ontario Building Code
Production: Print preparation, proofing, and vendor coordination

2.title: Translating Architectural Lines into a Distinct Typographic Voice
2.subtitle: Espacio Ideal
2.overview:
The Espacio Ideal Typeface builds on the studio’s architectural language, translating spatial thinking into typographic form. My focus was on capturing the rhythm, proportion, and balance found in their architectural sketches, turning hand-drawn gestures into a structured, functional design system. Using Illustrator and FontForge, I developed a framework that merges expressive line work with architectural precision, resulting in a typeface that feels both crafted and intentional. 

Throughout development, I studied how contrast, geometry, and negative space could echo the studio’s design principles: measured, deliberate, and enduring. What began as a personal exploration evolved into a working typeface now used as the foundation of Espacio Ideal’s rebrand. It anchors their new logo and visual identity across print and environmental applications, carrying forward the same clarity, rhythm, and material honesty that define their architectural work.
2.context:
The Espacio Ideal Typeface originated from a series of early collaborations with the studio, where architectural sketches often carried as much expression as the finished drawings. During one of these projects, the owner and architect shared a collection of hand-rendered studies that revealed a strong sense of rhythm and proportion, a set of architectural sketches defined by precision, gesture, and restraint. Those drawings became the foundation for exploring how the studio’s design sensibility could live beyond space and structure. 

Rather than replicate their work visually, the goal was to translate its essence, the balance between technical control and expressive freedom, into a typographic system. The process became a study in how architectural thinking can inform visual communication, and how their creative process reflects proportion, rhythm, and contrast with the application of shape not only for buildings but to letters. What began as a conceptual exercise evolved into a design direction that reinterprets Espacio Ideal’s architectural language through typography, setting the stage for what would later become a key element of their rebrand.
2.problem:
Espacio Ideal lacked a typographic voice that represented its architectural sophistication. 

their existing fonts felt either too generic, overly decorative, and inconsistent. Failing to express the studio’s balance of craft and clarity. The challenge was to develop a typographic system that functioned like architecture itself: rigorous in logic, restrained in detail, and built for longevity.
2.research: Through a detailed study of Espacio Ideal’s sketches, I identified recurring systems in how lines connected, intersected, and balanced proportionally. These became the structural DNA of the typeface, setting the logic and rhythm of each letterform. I observed that every architectural stroke carried weight and intention, a principle that guided the construction of the typeface with clarity and purpose. Repetition and proportion created a visual cadence essential for typographic balance, while the font’s character emerged not from decorative flourish, but from precision and restraint I added some unbalance to keep it fun. The process relied on the proper use of type guides and templates, referencing mood boards, and iterating through multiple tests in FontForge and across different media. Early print and screen proofs confirmed that optical balance often outweighed geometric accuracy, ensuring legibility and consistency across applications.
2.process: Designing architecture through letterforms, each stage echoed an architectural workflow: observation, structure, refinement, and material testing. Ensuring the typeface carried the integrity of its inspiration.
2.solution:
The Espacio Ideal Display Typeface is an all-caps system defined by linear precision, proportional discipline, and structural consistency. Designed to reflect the studio’s architectural approach, the typeface conveys confidence at large scales while revealing subtle craft and technical detail up close. Architectural grids and compositional logic informed these letterforms, giving rhythm and balance without compromising readability across applications. 

What began as a conceptual experiment became an essential part of Espacio Ideal’s renewed identity. The typeface now anchors logos, catalogues, and environmental graphics, uniting the studio’s design rigor with a contemporary typographic expression. Its structure allows for scalable growth, supporting future weights and variable font expansion, while performing seamlessly in print, digital, and environmental contexts.
2.impact:
The Espacio Ideal Display Typeface became more than a design exercise, it turned the studio’s architectural language into a functional, living typographic system. Grounded in proportion, rhythm, and structural logic, it now anchors their identity across print, digital, and environmental applications. 

Through this project, I learned to translate expressive sketches into a scalable digital system, gaining hands-on experience with FontForge, document setups, and type design workflows. The process reinforced the value of restraint, iterative refinement, and attention to detail, showing how a thoughtfully crafted system can communicate intention, support adoption, and endure alongside the studio it represents.
technologies: Design: Adobe Illustrator, FontForge, Procreate, Photoshop
Process Materials: Hand-rendered architectural drawings, vector grids, printed proofs
Testing Environments: Print proofs, on-screen mockups, brand collateral applications

3.title: Designing a Wine Experience that Blends Taste and Story
3.content: Wine Bottles Project for Weston Consulting.
3.subtitle: Weston Consulting
3.overview:
This project set out to create a gift that felt intentional and beautifully. By blending Renaissance artwork with Weston’s colour palette, the design transformed each bottle into a quiet, display‑worthy object. The objective was to design a collectible wine and packaging that embodied Weston Consulting’s values: warmth, sophistication, and gratitude, combining art direction, material craftsmanship, and narrative-driven design. 

The collection blended elegance, through adapted Renaissance artworks with Weston’s modern colour palette. This positioned the wine collection as a thoughtful representation of Weston’s commitment to meaningful client and employee relationships. The project aimed to create a refined, collectible wine gift that expressed gratitude through craftsmanship.
3.context:
Weston Consulting sought to elevate its annual appreciation program by moving beyond conventional corporate gifts and into a more intentional experience. The team wanted a gift that communicated gratitude, reflected the firm’s culture, and felt both personal and artfully crafted. Through this initiative, the wine collection became a symbolic gesture, one that celebrated relationships, craftsmanship, and the emotional nuance behind the firm’s work. 

As the project evolved, the wine collection was embraced not only as an internal gift but as a versatile expression of appreciation used for executive outreach, client milestones, and company-wide celebrations. Its success solidified it as a signature piece within Weston’s broader communication and gifting strategy. The solution became a limited‑edition wine and packaging collection, a warm, and art‑driven experience honouring the connection behind the company’s work. This pieces became Weston’s signature holiday gift for two consecutive years.
3.problem: Corporate gifts often default to predictable, forgettable formats, objects that check a box rather than communicate genuine appreciation. Weston Consulting wanted something different: a gift that reflected the firm’s character and felt designed rather than produced. The challenge was to build a visual experience that balanced subtle branding, artistic storytelling, and production realism without losing the warmth at the heart of the gesture.
3.research:
Research began by looking at how other firms approached corporate gifting, seasonal events, and client appreciation experiences. Many leaned on predictable motifs and overt branding, which felt impersonal and disconnected from the warmth Weston wanted to convey. Conversations with coordinators, leadership, and winery partners reinforced a shared desire for a gift that carried meaning, artistry, and a sense of care, something that felt timeless rather than seasonal. 

Studying industry gifting trends, seasonal event themes, and the visual language used across professional services revealed a clear opportunity: most gifts lacked emotional presence and artistic intention. Renaissance artwork introduced narrative depth, while Weston’s restrained palette kept the system modern and grounded. Material tests showed how subtle textures and finishes could elevate the experience without excess. Treating the bottles as limited-edition objects created a sense of significance that connected across audiences and occasions.
3.process: The project evolved through close coordination with leadership and the winery, moving from an initial concept rooted in the planning industry to a fully produced commemorative product. Each phase built on collaborative decision‑making, material testing, and iterative refinement.
3.solution: The final collection, an expression of appreciation, featured distinct wine bottles, inspired by classical portraiture, the other by Renaissance themes. Each was reinterpreted through modern restraint and Weston’s refined colour palette. Together, they formed a unified set that communicated warmth, gratitude, and artistry. A visual and sensory experience embodying the firm’s attention to detail and human connection.
3.impact:
This project successfully reframed Weston’s corporate gifting strategy, moving from inconsistent offerings to a curated, high-touch experience. It strengthened stakeholder and management relationships and was adopted as the official corporate gift for two consecutive years, establishing a successful and repeatable program. By coordinating the production and logistics for a substantial volume, the project increased brand visibility, featuring prominently at multiple corporate events. The result garnered enthusiastic feedback company wide and external, reinforcing Weston’s commitment to design-driven appreciation. 

The process was a great experience and way in mastering interdisciplinary coordination and logistics. My study of material and production timelines provided a nuanced understanding of supply chain relationships. Managing and coordinating multiple external vendors (winery, printers, fulfillment) reinforced the importance of proactive alignment to avoid bottlenecks, highlighting that understanding the craft of external partners is essential to success. The project affirmed the value of logistical precision and intention, ensuring 100% on-time delivery for a critical corporate distribution window.
technologies: Design: Adobe Illustrator, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe InDesign
Production: Material sourcing, print finishing, vendor coordination
3.team: Designer, Office Coordinator, Local Winery Partner

4.title: Wild Lines of Stratford: A Wildlife-Inspired Beer Label Series for a Seasonal Brew
4.subtitle: Burlington Co.
4.overview:
Wild Lines of Stratford, a series of beer can labels created for a local brewery, translates local wildlife into a packaging system defined by geometric, angular illustration rendered in stark white-on-black contrast, infused with a personal illustrative style inspired by Alberto Giacometti. Three animals central to Stratford's environment: fox, swan, and racoons, are rendered through a single line, crystalline linework that echoes Giacometti's abstraction. 

Using Procreate to create these geometric drawings and Adobe Illustrator and InDesign for composition refinement, I created labels, and a small custom iconic that reinforces brand identity. The dark finish contrasting on the aluminum cans serve as a bold backdrop, allowing the white illustrations to command attention on shelf while communicating the intensity of the brewery's darker seasonal beer.
4.context:
Wild Lines of Stratford began as a self-directed exploration and then proposal, translating local wildlife into geometric, angular illustration inspired by Giacometti's sculptural forms. After a brief visit and conversation with Burlington Beers Co., known for collaborating with local artists, saw potential in the work and adopted the series for their darker seasonal brew, a beer whose bold character matched the stark contrast and expressive linework. 

The collaboration transformed conceptual work into thematic packaging. The can surface became a canvas for white line illustrations, with label wording, regulatory information, and a custom icon system integrated. Through iterative feedback and production adjustments, the series evolved into three labels that balanced artistic expression with commercial requirements.
4.problem: Burlington Beers Co. sought fresh packaging for their winter seasonal release: a series of darker, bolder brews that needed visual identity reflecting both the season's character and the brewery's commitment to local artistry. I developed a proposal centred on Stratford's wildlife, translated through geometric illustration that captured winter's stark beauty and the beer's intensity.
4.research: The foundation of this project came from direct observation and artistic exploration. Walking through Stratford, I identified the most commonly seen animals: swans, foxes, and raccoons, that could serve as recognizable local symbols. My fascination with Alberto Giacometti's sculptural work at the time drove the visual direction, leading me to study his approach to form, proportion, and the energy of fragmented, angular lines. Later on and after proposal there sessions flavour positioning and label copy.
4.process: The design process unfolded over five months, moving through distinct phases that refined the balance between artistic exploration and functional packaging. Each stage built upon the previous, transitioning from personal study to collaborative refinement with Burlington Beers Co.
4.solution: The final design delivers three cohesive labels that function as bold visual statements on black aluminum cans. Each features geometric wildlife illustrations rendered in crisp white single-line compositions, paired with clean typography and a distinctive custom icon. The monochromatic approach creates immediate shelf impact while establishing a visual identity that feels intentional, contemporary, and connected to Stratford's environment.
4.impact:
Reaching out to Burlington Beers Co. transformed an academic exercise into real-world application, revealing how networking and confident presentation can materialize concepts into tangible outcomes. The experience of pitching work, articulating design rationale, and positioning the proposal as a solution built skills that extended far beyond the classroom. Collaborating with the brewery reinforced the balance between vision and flexibility. Meetings and comments required navigating feedback while protecting core design decisions. Learning when to defend choices and when to adapt strengthened my ability to work professionally without compromising artistic direction. 

Witnessing the complete lifecycle, from observing wildlife in Stratford to holding finished cans, was transformative and exciting. That experience shifted my understanding of design from academic exercises to meaningful practice, reinforcing that creating something people interact with in the real world carries way more satisfaction that renders and mockups cannot replicate.
technologies: Design: Procreate, Adobe Illustrator, Adobe InDesign
Production: Print specifications, colour proofing, label die-cut templates
Process Materials: Wildlife sketches, line work studies

5.title: Autonomous X Artists: Transforming Workspaces Through Illustrated Design
5.subtitle: Autonomous.ai (Project A²)
5.overview:
Autonomous.ai specializes in ergonomic office solutions, building standing desks and smart furniture designed to support healthier, more productive work environments. The Autonomous X Artists collaboration sought to bring creative expression into this utilitarian space, transforming their SmartDesk line into limited-edition art pieces through Project A². 

For this project I developed an illustration that combined clean lines, vibrant colour palettes, and playful composition. My design was created as a fun addition to the desk surface. Ultimately demonstrating that workspace tools could serve as vehicles for personal expression. The project reinforced my belief that design can elevate everyday objects into meaningful experiences. By contributing to the Project A² collection, I participated in a broader conversation about the role of creativity in professional environments and the potential for art to make workspaces more personal, engaging, and inspiring.
5.context:
The Autonomous X Artists collaboration emerged from Autonomous's vision to redefine the workspace through the integration of art and function. Project A² elevated the SmartDesk from a utilitarian object into a canvas for creative expression, partnering with emerging international artists to bring unique visual voices to everyday office furniture. The initiative aimed to challenge the traditional perception of work environments as sterile, impersonal spaces by introducing personalized, vibrant design into the fundamental tool of productivity: the standing desk. 

This collaboration represented an opportunity to merge illustration with industrial design, transforming a mass-produced product into a limited-edition piece of functional art. The project culminated in a special edition auction and product line, positioning these illustrated desks as collectible objects. What began as a surface design challenge evolved into an exploration of how art can reshape the relationship between individuals and their workspaces.
5.problem:
Traditional office furniture operates within a narrow aesthetic vocabulary: neutral, minimal, and intentionally forgettable. While functional, these design choices often result in workspaces that feel impersonal and disconnected from the individuals who occupy them. For creative professionals and those seeking to personalize their environments, the standard standing desk offered no opportunity for self-expression, visual identity or colour. 

Autonomous recognized this gap between function and personalization. Their SmartDesk line delivered ergonomic performance and quality construction but lacked the distinctive character that would allow users to connect emotionally with their workspace. The challenge was to introduce artistic expression into a product category dominated by utilitarian design without compromising the desk's functional requirements or professional appearance.
5.research: The layout was structured using accessible typography, a clear visual hierarchy, and a modular template to ensure consistency and efficient rollout. Visual elements, including a custom-designed map, were created to meet accessibility guidelines and enhance clarity. Integrated QR codes allow for extended digital engagement, and the final piece was printed on recyclable stock, reinforcing sustainable design practices.
5.process: The design process unfolded through close collaboration with Autonomous, moving from conceptual exploration to production-ready artwork. Each phase built on feedback and technical understanding, allowing the illustration to evolve while maintaining clear direction toward creating a desk that celebrated youth culture and personal expression.
5.solution:
The final illustrations transformed the SmartDesk surface into a canvas for creative expression while maintaining full functionality as a workspace tool. The design elevated the desk from furniture to a statement piece that resonated with creative young people, demonstrating that workspace tools could carry personal meaning while maintaining practical purpose. Clean lines, intentional colour palettes, and thoughtful placement ensured the designs read clearly at full scale without overwhelming the space. 

By participating in the Project A² auction format, these illustrated desks became limited-edition collectibles, merging the worlds of functional design and fine art. The project successfully demonstrated that workspaces could be both highly functional and deeply personal, offering users an opportunity to invest in objects that inspire creativity while serving practical needs.
5.impact:
The Autonomous X Artists collaboration validated the idea that art belongs everywhere, not just in galleries or designated creative spaces. By bringing illustration into the workspace, the collaboration helped normalize the integration of creativity into daily professional life, suggesting that the environments we work in can be both productive and inspiring. 

Working with Autonomous's production team taught me to bridge creative vision with manufacturing constraints, understanding how digital artwork translates to physical products. Participating in this initiative reinforced my understanding of design as a problem-solving discipline that extends beyond visual appeal. Creating artwork for a functional product requires different considerations than gallery work, demanding awareness of user interaction, durability, production constraints, and long-term visual sustainability. 

Seeing these designs become objects that people could own, use, and connect with daily was deeply rewarding, affirming the power of design to enhance lived experience in tangible, meaningful ways.
technologies: Design: Procreate, Adobe Illustrator, Adobe Photoshop
Production: High-quality digital printing process, colour calibration
Process Materials: Concept sketches, colour studies, functional design testing and coordination

6.title: POSS Magazine: A Minimalist Editorial Exploration of Urban Culture
6.subtitle: YGTUT, Humble Magazine
6.overview:
POSS Magazine operates as a curated editorial object where typography, imagery, and cultural narrative converge into a disciplined visual system. Rooted in my experience growing up in Colombia, the magazine draws from the rhythms, tensions, and aesthetics of urban life, translating them into a minimal, gallery-like print language. The goal was not only to showcase imagery, but to build a refined editorial framework capable of elevating everyday cultural expression into a contemplative visual experience. 

The magazine functions as a series of controlled visual moments, balanced compositions, quiet grids, and measured contrasts, all working together to create an intentional narrative rhythm. Each spread serves as an independent visual object with its own tone and theme, yet all are unified through a shared aesthetic logic and layout. This systematic approach transformed the publication into more than a promotional artifact; POSS became a portable, minimal art piece that reflects both personal cultural perspective and contemporary urban movement.
6.context:
POSS Magazine began as a self-initiated exploration of urban culture, minimalism, and editorial design, inspired by the experiences and personal memories of my upbringing in Colombia. Unlike conventional fashion or lifestyle publications, it was conceived as a portable art object: a curated system where each spread is treated as a gallery-like composition with intentional pacing and rhythm. 

The project emerged from early experiments with social media traction, validating the potential of this editorial approach and leading to opportunities for collaboration. The print templates were eventually acquired by Humble Magazine, a U.S-based virtual publication, and became a gateway to further creative projects, including marketing visual work for the rapper YGTUT. Programs such as Adobe Photoshop, Illustrator, and InDesign were leveraged to craft imagery, develop layouts, and maintain a consistent, minimalist aesthetic. The careful arrangement of typography, imagery, and spacing created an editorial framework that could flexibly communicate a variety of themes while maintaining cohesion and narrative clarity.
6.problem:
Urban visual culture often defaults to a loud, maximalist aesthetic: high saturation, dense compositions, and overwhelming layouts that value impact over intention. Having grown up surrounded by the textures and contradictions of Colombian urban life, I saw an opportunity to reinterpret this energy through a different lens: a form of disorderly minimalism. 

Rather than silencing the urban essence, this approach aimed to refine it, maintaining its authenticity while removing unnecessary excess. The goal was to create a minimalist identity that still felt distinctly urban, where every element had purpose and tension. Existing publications in the space lacked this balance, relying on unrefined imagery, inconsistent typographic systems, and cluttered visual languages that diluted the message. POSS Magazine set out to redefine how urban culture could be expressed through print: intentional, measured, and visually restrained without compromising spirit.
6.research:
Early research into contemporary Colombian urban aesthetics showed a heavy reliance on saturation, layered effects, a maximalist approach that often diluted the authenticity of the message behind it. This contrast made it clear that POSS needed to pursue a different direction: a cleaner, sharper visual strategy capable of preserving urban identity without the surrounding noise. 

I explored minimalist editorial references, from Swiss and Bauhaus systems to high-fashion print structures (American and European styles) to understand how spacing, contrast, and typographic discipline could reframe urban expression. Through moodboards, typographic tests, and multiple refinements, I found that intentional minimialism was the correct approach, bringing clarity and emotional weight to the imagery. These insights established the foundation for POSS Magazine’s visual language: a restrained, precise system where urban culture is elevated through structure, rhythm, and visual silence.
6.process:
The creation of POSS Magazine unfolded over nine months, evolving from a conjunct editorial exploration with another designer into a multi-stage project involving publication and artist collaboration. The early months focused on research, experimentation, and developing a visual language. As the system matured, through iterations of layout, imagery treatment, and typographic refinement, the magazine took form as a cohesive, minimal editorial object grounded in clarity and cultural intent. 

Once the magazine was completed, momentum grew through deliberate posting, visual teasers, and small social media experiments intended to build presence around the project. This effort led to a collaboration with Humble Magazine, who adapted the templates for their editorial use. The project expanded again when we reached out to YGTUT, an artist whose work had influenced me deeply. After sending samples, we began developing a collage-based campaign, working directly with his management and YGTUT himself. This final phase marked the shift from personal project to collaborative output.
6.solution:
The magazine emerged as a disciplined editorial system rooted from clarity, structure, and minimal visual language. The final publication operated less like a traditional magazine and more like a curated art object, conceived to be a piece that complements a space. This refined aesthetic became central to its impact. The cohesive template system translated smoothly into Humble Magazine’s editorial workflow, offering them a more structured and elevated visual direction for their content. The same design logic extended into digital and social formats, ultimately shaping the collage-driven campaign developed for YGTUT. Working with his management and securing direct approvals from the artist, the visuals maintained the magazine’s minimalist tension while adapting to a more expressive musical context. 

POSS proved capable of moving across mediums: print, publication, social media, and artist promotional material, while consistently preserving the identity and restraint that defined its original concept. Its foundational principles of structure and measured composition now guide future applications.
6.impact:
POSS Magazine successfully reframed how urban culture could be presented, shifting from chaotic visuals to a curated system grounded in minimalism and structure. The unique visual identity proved to be a valuable asset, leading to the acquisition of its design templates by Humble Magazine. This collaboration achieved international traction, expanding the project's visibility into the U.S. creative and music spaces. The project also generated significant buzz, reaching 1,000+ engagements across social platforms. Most importantly, the established design credibility led to graphic collaboration with rapper YGTUT (30k+ audience), delivering design solutions that reached a significantly larger audience and solidified my professional brand within the music culture landscape. 

The project reaffirmed the value of restraint and intentional reduction in editorial design. The process deepened my understanding of digital publications as a powerful communication medium. Beyond the technical skills, the work reinforced the importance of client-facing expertise: learning how to effectively sell a product, present complex ideas, and successfully navigate client meetings to secure buy-in and manage expectations. Rooted in the discipline of strong grid compositions, the work highlighted typography's emotional influence and reaffirmed that design, when executed with clarity, can simultaneously honour minimalism and expressive cultural storytelling.
technologies: Design: Adobe InDesign, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Illustrator, Figma
Production: Color palette studies, image treatment workflows, layout templates, marketing research
Process Materials: Moodboards, photography references, typographic & layout studies
6.team: Independent Designer, Design Partner, Magazine Editorial Team, Musical Artist & Management

7.title: Weston Consulting X Waterfirst: Run, Ride or Walk
7.content: The Run, Ride or Walk project for Weston Consulting.
7.subtitle: Weston Consulting
7.overview:
This project centred on creating a shirt design for Weston Consulting’s participation in a 5km fundraising run in support of Water First, an organization dedicated to improving access to safe, clean water in Indigenous communities across Canada. The design needed to be direct, uplifting, and easy to understand, ensuring the message of the event: movement with purpose, was instantly recognizable. 

To achieve this, I used the form of a shoe sole as the core motif, symbolizing running, riding, and walking in one unified gesture. Paired with a friendly, energetic colour palette and clean custom typography, the final design showcased a visual identity that felt fun, approachable, and suitable for both company participants and campaign visibility. As part of the fundraiser merchandise, the shirt helped create cohesion at the event and social media while highlighting the mission behind the effort.
7.context: The “Run, Ride, or Walk” campaign brought together Weston Consulting and Water First to raise awareness and support for clean water initiatives across Indigenous communities. I was responsible for creating the event’s official shirt design, an opportunity to develop a visual identity that felt energetic, meaningful, and tailored to a broad community-focused audience.
7.problem: The campaign needed a shirt design that not only represented the slogan “Run, Ride, or Walk” event but also visually aligned both Weston Consulting and Water First under a single cohesive identity. Typical charity event shirts often lean on predictable visual cues or generic athletic motifs; however, this collaboration required movement, unity, and purpose without relying on overly literal or conventional graphics. The design needed to stand out in a crowded landscape of community event apparel while remaining accessible to a wide demographic of participants of all ages.
7.research:
The research phase focused on understanding how to communicate motion: running, riding, and walking, through a single graphic that could remain clear, friendly, and instantly readable on a shirt. Instead of studying user demographics or brand perception, the investigation centred on visual language: how shapes, forms, and composition could express movement in a simple, unified illustration. 

I explored imagery related to athletic motion, reviewing various sole patterns, dynamic line compositions, and abstract forms commonly used in event branding. This included testing multiple styles ranging from literal depictions of footwear to more abstract patterns that suggested forward momentum. Through sketching in Procreate, I iterated on different silhouettes and graphic treatments to determine which approach communicated activity most effectively without adding unnecessary visual complexity.
7.process: The creation of the fundraising shirt followed an iterative, detail‑driven process focused on expressing movement clearly and producing a graphic that would print cleanly across both shirt colourways. The workflow moved from initial sketching to vector refinement, type customization, colour matching, and final coordination with Waterfirst’s production requirements.
7.solution: The final “Run, Ride, or Walk” shirt design is a dynamic yet approachable composition built around custom illustration, pastel colour choices, and clean typographic identity. The shoe‑sole‑inspired shapes create a sense of movement and connection, celebrating the ways people come together in support of Water First’s mission.
7.impact:
The final shirt design successfully met the campaign’s goal of creating a recognizable, uplifting, and movement-focused identity for the “Run, Ride, or Walk” initiative. Leadership at Weston Consulting expressed strong satisfaction with the final outcome, highlighting how the illustration communicated motion, purpose, and alignment with Water First’s mission. Early coordination with the printing team ensured the artwork translated accurately to fabric, preserving the clarity of line work and the softness of the palette. 

By working from an abstract yet meaningful foundation, the sole of a shoe, I learned to balance symbolism with visual clarity, crafting a design that felt both expressive and accessible. The process deepened my ability to translate hand-drawn concepts into production-ready assets and underscored the importance of clear communication when collaborating. The positive reception from Weston’s leadership further affirmed the value of thoughtful design in amplifying the impact of mission-centred initiatives.
technologies: Design: Adobe Illustrator, Adobe InDesign, Adobe Photoshop, Procreate
Typography: Custom font exploration
Colour: Pantone Color Matching

8.title: Designing a Green Standards Toolkit for Sustainable & Accessible Urban Practice
8.content: Green Standards Toolkit for Weston Consulting.
8.subtitle: Weston Consulting
8.overview:
The Green Standards Toolkit is a guide created to promote sustainable urban development through clear, engaging design. Developed in collaboration with a senior urban designer and an architect, the toolkit communicates complex ideas through layered diagrams, strategic layouts, and accessible formatting, all aligned with AODA standards to ensure broad usability. 

As part of Weston Consulting’s initiative to unify its sustainable design practice, the Green Standards Toolkit was developed to guide internal teams of architects and urban designers toward a shared visual and technical language. This manual consolidates sustainable design standards, principles, and technical drawing conventions into a single, accessible framework, making it easier for teams to maintain visual consistency, clarity, and compliance across all projects.
8.context:
The Green Standards Toolkit builds on Weston’s goal of aligning sustainability with visual communication. My focus was on translating technical information into a design system that feels approachable and cohesive. Using a the company’s existing typographic structure with Arial in varied weights, and a nature-inspired yet high-contrast colour palette, the toolkit showcases clarity with visual rhythm. 

Throughout development, I worked closely with the design team to refine plan markups, symbols, and diagrams, creating a unified visual logic that links environmental data, architectural detail, and spatial representation. The result is more than a manual, it’s a visual language that brings familiarity and ambiance to technical design, helping teams communicate sustainable principles with confidence and precision. The toolkit continues to be used today as a foundation for Weston’s sustainable design materials and internal standards.
8.problem: With the team producing multiple technical drawings and planning documents, the company needed a unified approach to maintain visual quality, accessibility, and sustainability alignment. We were tasked to create a toolkit that simplifies communication, and standardize visual output.
8.research:
Building a Shared Design Language. Through internal analysis, we identified the need for a consistent visual system that connects planning, architecture, and communication.

I used Arial in different weights to keep layouts clean and readable, balancing clarity with hierarchy. The colour palette: greens, blue, yellow, and grey, takes cues from natural tones to build familiarity and ambiance while maintaining strong accessibility contrast. Plan markups, icons, and tree and people models bring rhythm and legibility to technical drawings. A custom illustration I created during the research phase became the visual anchor for this system, it was used as the cover and later adopted by Weston for other design deliverables. Together, these elements form a clear, accessible, and unified visual language that ties design logic to real environments.
8.process: Designing a toolkit that draws connection between disciplines.
8.solution: A unified visual and technical framework for sustainable design. The final Green Standards Toolkit establishes a shared design language that aligns technical drawing standards, accessibility principles, and sustainable design guidelines. It functions as both a visual system and a technical manual, ensuring that every diagram, layout, and illustration across Weston Consulting reflects clarity, sustainability, and compliance.
8.impact:
The toolkit became a key internal reference for Weston Consulting, improving consistency across urban design and architecture projects while raising awareness of AODA standards. It strengthened collaboration between designers, architects, and planners, and laid the groundwork for future digital tools and training. 

Through this process, I learned how design can translate technical information into something clear, accessible, and engaging. I discovered that translation goes beyond language, that consistency, sharpness, and purpose in design can create meaningful results and experiences. Aligning sustainability, accessibility, and visual precision turned the Green Standards Toolkit into more than a document, it became a shared language across disciplines. It also taught me to design for adoption, creating systems that others can use, expand, and evolve long after the project ends.
technologies: Design: Adobe InDesign, Adobe Illustrator, Adobe Photoshop, Procreate
Accessibility & Standards: AODA, WCAG 2.1, Ontario Building Code
Visualization: AutoCAD (3D modeling, in collaboartion with Architect)

11.title: A Catalogue Series that Reframed a Studio’s Identity
11.subtitle: Espacio Ideal
11.overview:
The Catalogue Series translates Espacio Ideal’s architectural principles into a tactile editorial system. My focus centred on transforming spatial logic: proportion, rhythm, and material contrast, into a cohesive print language that felt intentional, and aligned with the studio’s ethos. 

Using Adobe InDesign, Illustrator & Photoshop, I developed a system defined by quiet and sharp typography, measured spacing, and a disciplined balance between sketches, photography, and material texture. Each catalogue functioned as an independent object with its own narrative purpose, yet all were unified through a shared logic that echoed Espacio Ideal’s architectural clarity. What began as a systematic exploration of form and sequence ultimately became the foundation for Espacio Ideal’s broader communication style. The Catalogue Series established the visual rhythm and editorial tone that later guided the studio’s digital transformation, providing a material-first blueprint for how their craft is communicated across mediums.
11.context:
The Catalogue Series emerged at a pivotal moment for Espacio Ideal, a studio defined by thirty years of architectural craft yet represented by materials that no longer reflected its precision. Early conversations with the lead architect revealed a desire for a printed system that felt intentional, curated, and capable of communicating the emotional weight and tightness of their work. The studio’s existing materials (PDFs) mismatched presentations, these aging catalogues fell short of expressing the clarity and restraint that guided their architectural thinking. 

Rather than produce another promotional booklet, the goal was to create a system of objects, each built with the same care the studio applies to its spaces. These catalogues became a study in proportion, rhythm, and materiality, not only as decorative gestures, but as structural components that communicated identity. What began as a print redesign evolved into the foundation for Espacio Ideal’s broader rebrand, establishing a visual language that translated into digital form.
11.problem: Espacio Ideal lacked printed materials capable of expressing the sophistication and intentionality of its current architectural practice. The existing catalogues diluted the studio’s identity, presenting projects in a fragmented, inconsistent manner. The materials were dense with information yet unorganized, making them difficult to navigate for RFPs, company presentations, and client-facing communications. Without a clear system, the studio’s work failed to reflect the precision, and thoughtfulness inherent in their craft. The challenge was to create a printed editorial system that mirrored the studio’s design ethos: coherent, intentional, and engaging, while serving as a functional tool for presenting complex projects.
11.research:
Through interviews and early design workshops, I identified recurring themes in how the team approached space, material, and proportion, questioning what they’d like to see as a result of this project, types of clients and audience. Their architectural process relied heavily on rhythm and restraint, qualities absent from their printed materials. This understanding guided the design: the catalogues needed to feel calm, intentional, and materially honest. 

I studied how print finishing, paper texture, and scale could echo the studio’s design ethos, drawing inspiration from Paul Rand’s early work, use of white space and a way of obtaining gigantic results with proper use of design principles, researched on Ikea’s catalogue systems to study how information was displayed, also studying from the architect’s favourite printed materials, some of them being bauhaus produced. Early proofs revealed that small refinements, small margins adjustments, softened contrast, quiet grids, and a defined design approach and colour palette, created a sense of balance that matched their architectural language. These insights shaped a catalogue system where material, sequence, and proportion carried equal weight.
11.process: The Catalogue Series took shape through the same logic the studio uses in its architecture practices, observation, understanding, and intent. I started by studying their past materials and speaking with the team to understand how they wanted their work to feel, which helped define the principles of proportion, rhythm, and pacing that guided the system. From there, I created a grid and a flexible InDesign setup that could handle future updates without losing structure. We tested layouts together, refining how images, text, and white space interacted until the catalogues felt balanced and purposeful. Material testing became its own design phase. Working with a local print shop, we compared papers, embossing depths, foils, and finishes, looking for the combination that best reflected the studio’s detail-driven approach. The final stretch focused on polish: copy revisions, refining imagery, preparing files for production, and walking the team through how to maintain and update the system. The goal was not just to deliver a set of catalogues, but a framework the studio could continue to build on.
11.solution:
The Catalogue Series became a set of printed publications that captured Espacio Ideal’s commitment to material precision and architectural clarity. Each piece functions as objects proportioned with intention, spacious in its composition, and restrained in its detail. Quiet typography, balanced imagery, and pacing form the visual logic of the system, giving every catalogue a consistent tone and sense of structure. 

Built to evolve with the studio, the series now acts as both a promotional tool and a core expression of their identity. Its structure allows projects to be added or reorganized without losing coherence, while material choices give the catalogues the tactile quality that defines their work. The design principles established here became the foundation for the broader rebrand, guiding future digital and print applications with the same clarity and discipline.
11.impact:
The Catalogue Series reframed how Espacio Ideal communicated its work, shifting from inconsistent materials to a curated system grounded in proportion and craft. It strengthened the relationship between the studio and its clients, increased project turnaround efficiency, and created a precise, engaging experience for each client. Most importantly, it brought to life the ideas of another creative, delivering results the studio could proudly present and showcase to the world. The project became the foundation for the studio’s evolving brand identity, demonstrating how tactile design can guide and strengthen digital expression. 

The process deepened my understanding of print as a communication medium, where pacing, sequence, and material shape perception as powerfully as form and current web practices. Rooted in Swiss design principles, my study of patterns, primary shapes, and grid compositions provided guidance and a nuanced understanding of spatial relationships. Collaborating with a print shop reinforced the importance of material, printing, and color, highlighting that understanding the craft of others is as essential as mastering your own. The project reaffirmed the value of restraint and the impact of designing with intention.

12.title: Rebranding a Legacy Studio into a Curated Digital Experience
12.subtitle: Espacio Ideal
12.overview:
The new Espacio Ideal website extends the logic of the Catalogue Series into a fully digital experience, translating the studio’s material-driven identity into an online environment that feels quiet, intentional, and grounded. Where the catalogues established a tactile editorial rhythm, the website carries that system forward, using motion, spacing, and compositional restraint that create continuity and consistency. The work remains anchored to their roots. 

Built as both a portfolio and an operational tool, the site introduces pathways for appointment scheduling, project inquiries, and client communication. Subtle animations were created to complement, not overshadow, the architectural work, introducing movement and interactivity while preserving the minimalist clarity that defines the brand. This shift reduces the need for in-person interactions and allows the studio to remain active and accessible while working abroad. As Espacio Ideal embraces digital transformation, the website becomes a natural evolution of the Catalogue Series, supporting business operations, elevating the client experience, and marking a confident step into a modern, technology-integrated era for the studio.
12.context:
For over a decade, Espacio Ideal operated without a digital presence, relying entirely on word-of-mouth and direct relationships. While this reflected the studio's deliberate ethos, it confined their reach to an existing circle, limiting growth and making remote engagement impossible. The website emerged as the studio's first digital platform, conceived not as a departure but as a natural extension of their values. Early discussions revealed the need for a system that could express architectural precision and facilitate client communication while preserving the intimacy that defines their practice. 

Rather than building a promotional site, the goal became creating a digital environment mirroring the studio's approach to proportion, rhythm, and restraint. Central to this vision were the architect's hand-drawn sketches: quiet, gestural visuals that carry personal warmth. These drawings, paired with clean compositional systems and subtle motion, form the foundation of the experience, ensuring the site feels less like a corporate portfolio and more like a direct conversation between architect and client, a visual gallery experience. This project translates the material and editorial rigour of the Catalogue Series into an interactive medium, one that allows Espacio Ideal to present work thoughtfully, engage clients remotely, and operate seamlessly while maintaining the architectural craft at the heart of the brand.
12.problem: Espacio Ideal lacked a digital platform capable of expressing the sophistication and intentionality of its architectural practice. The previous website, built over a decade ago, presented work in a generic, uninspired manner that failed to reflect the studio's evolving identity. As part of a broader company rebrand, the studio was positioning itself to step into a more curatorial role, setting design trends, offering architectural guidance, and establishing a distinct point of view within the industry. Without a digital presence that embodied this vision, the studio remained invisible to potential clients outside their immediate network and unable to communicate their approach. Navigation was unclear, the visual system felt disconnected, and there was no mechanism to guide or qualify incoming inquiries. Operational workflows were inefficient, relying on manual processes that couldn't scale. The challenge was to create a digital system that mirrored the studio's design ethos: precise, restrained, and now curatorial, while functioning as both a digital catalogue and an operational tool that could support their transformation into industry and local architecture leaders.
12.research: The research phase involved analyzing competitor architectural portfolios, conducting interviews with the internal team, and mapping the client journey from initial inquiry to project engagement. Competitor analysis revealed a trend toward overly complex, image-heavy portfolios that prioritized aesthetic spectacle over clarity and function. Meanwhile, conversations with the team exposed operational bottlenecks: hours spent answering repetitive material questions, scheduling conflicts handled manually, and a lack of preparation to meet client preferences kick off meetings. Mapping the client journey uncovered critical friction points: prospective clients had no way to understand the their process, explore material options, or communicate their vision before the first conversation, leading to misaligned expectations and wasted discovery time. Additionally, the studio's aspiration to position itself as a curatorial voice in the industry required a platform that could house editorial content, showcase imagery, and evolve independently without external dependencies. These findings pointed toward a need for a self-guided client experience, operational automation, and a content management system that empowered the team to maintain momentum.
12.process:
I started by analyzing competitor sites and speaking with the team to understand how they wanted their work to be experienced digitally. This helped define the principles that would guide the system: clarity, restraint, and a balance between editorial control and functional simplicity. The goal was to create a platform that felt like a natural extension of their architectural work, measured, intentional, and built to evolve. 

From there, I mapped the information architecture and built wireframes that prioritized user flow and content hierarchy. We worked through how clients would navigate services, explore projects, and engage with materials, refining the structure until it felt intuitive. Visual design followed, translating the catalogue's typographic rules and spatial logic into React components. The architect's hand-drawn sketches became focal points, personal, balanced against clean layouts and generous whitespace. I tested how motion could enhance the experience without overwhelming it, calibrating animations to feel architectural: subtle, dimensional, purposeful. 

Development was built around long-term maintainability and flexibility. Using React and Tailwind, I created a component-driven architecture designed to support updates and growth. The final phase focused on refinement: testing interactions, optimizing performance, and ensuring the system could adapt as the studio's needs evolve. The platform remains active, with ongoing updates and improvements.
12.solution:
The final website became a digital system that extends Espacio Ideal's architectural precision into an interactive platform. Structured around the same compositional logic as the Catalogue Series, the site balances editorial restraint with operational functionality, creating a curated environment where clients can explore work, understand services, and initiate contact with clarity and intention. 

Hand-drawn sketches anchor the visual experience, offering clean and spacious layouts. the introduction of GSAP animations give the site a subtle dimensional shifts that guide attention without distraction, mirroring the rhythm and proportion found in the studio's physical work and my previous collaborations with them. The booking flow filters inquiries upfront, improving lead quality and aligning expectations before the first conversation. Built with React and Tailwind, the component-driven architecture ensures long-term flexibility, allowing the studio to expand and refine the platform as their practice evolves, providing a scalable and low-cost solution.
12.impact:
The website transformed how Espacio Ideal connects with clients, replacing manual processes with a self-guided digital experience that reflects the studio's precision. Early metrics suggest a 25% increase in high-quality inquiries, with clearer expectations set before initial consultations. The component-driven architecture enabled the team to manage content autonomously, eliminating external dependencies and allowing the studio to maintain momentum while working abroad. The platform became the digital anchor for the broader rebrand, demonstrating how the Catalogue Series' principles could translate seamlessly into an interactive medium. 

The project reinforced that digital experiences can carry the same emotional resonance as physical materials when built with restraint and intention. Motion along subtle transitions became a tool to guide attention without overwhelming the us. Designing for long-term flexibility revealed the importance of system thinking: a strong component architecture and unified design language create foundations that support growth without sacrificing coherence. The continuity between print and digital systems proved essential; when both are built from shared principles, they strengthen rather than dilute each other.
